claim: NRSF mRNA expression levels increase following KA-induced seizures in vivo.
source: (A) Time-course of NRSF mRNA expression levels following KA-induced seizures, n = 4/group.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing time-dependent increases in NRSF mRNA levels after KA-induced seizures, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NRSF protein levels increase at 72 hours post KA-induced seizures.
source: Quantification of NRSF protein levels using optical density measurements (ctrl 1.96 ± 0.18, n = 6; KA+72hr 6.75 ± 0.54, n = 3; KA+1 week: 5.42 ± 0.36, n = 3).
evidence: Western blot analysis with quantification shows NRSF protein levels increased approximately 3.4-fold at 72 hours after KA-induced seizures compared to controls.

claim: NRSF protein levels increase at 1 week post KA-induced seizures.
source: Quantification of NRSF protein levels using optical density measurements (ctrl 1.96 ± 0.18, n = 6; KA+72hr 6.75 ± 0.54, n = 3; KA+1 week: 5.42 ± 0.36, n = 3).
evidence: Western blot analysis with quantification shows NRSF protein levels increased approximately 2.8-fold at 1 week after KA-induced seizures compared to controls.

claim: KA induces seizure-like electrophysiological events in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures.
source: KA provoked seizure-like electrophysiological events in the hippocampal slice (Richichi et al., 2008) and led a to time-dependent increase of NRSF mRNA and protein levels (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richichi et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: KA treatment leads to time-dependent increase of NRSF mRNA levels in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures.
source: KA provoked seizure-like electrophysiological events in the hippocampal slice (Richichi et al., 2008) and led a to time-dependent increase of NRSF mRNA and protein levels (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data in organotypic cultures shows time-dependent increases in NRSF mRNA at 4hr, 12hr, 24hr, and 1 week following KA treatment.

claim: NRSF mRNA levels increase in CA1 pyramidal cell layer following KA-induced seizure-like events in organotypic cultures.
source: Quantification of mRNA in pyramidal cell layer was performed in control cultures as well as cultures 4 hr, 12 hr, 24 hr, and 1 week following seizure-like events in CA1 and CA3 region of the hippocampus, n = 4–8/group, *p<0.05.
evidence: In situ hybridization with quantification shows statistically significant increases in NRSF mRNA in CA1 pyramidal cell layer at multiple time points after KA treatment.

claim: NRSF mRNA levels increase in CA3 pyramidal cell layer following KA-induced seizure-like events in organotypic cultures.
source: Quantification of mRNA in pyramidal cell layer was performed in control cultures as well as cultures 4 hr, 12 hr, 24 hr, and 1 week following seizure-like events in CA1 and CA3 region of the hippocampus, n = 4–8/group, *p<0.05.
evidence: In situ hybridization with quantification shows statistically significant increases in NRSF mRNA in CA3 pyramidal cell layer at multiple time points after KA treatment.

claim: Expression of 12,996 genes was detected in the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus.
source: Expression of 12,996 genes was detected in the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus of which 371 (2.8%) contained NRSE sites (Johnson et al., 2007).
evidence: Microarray analysis detected this number of expressed genes in hippocampal CA1 region.

claim: 371 genes (2.8% of detected genes) in rat hippocampal CA1 contain NRSE sites.
source: Expression of 12,996 genes was detected in the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus of which 371 (2.8%) contained NRSE sites (Johnson et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on microarray detection and NRSE site identification from Johnson et al., 2007.

claim: 470 genes were significantly repressed by KA-induced seizures in hippocampal CA1.
source: 470 genes whose expression was significantly repressed by KA-induced seizures were identified by this initial candidate gene analysis that employed routine statistical significance (Subramanian et al., 2005; Yukhananov and Kissin, 2008; Borg et al., 2010; Oberbauer et al., 2010; Stark et al., 2010).
evidence: Microarray analysis with statistical testing identified 470 genes with significantly repressed expression after KA-induced seizures.

claim: 39 genes (8.3%) of the 470 seizure-repressed genes contain NRSF binding sites.
source: Of these, 39 (8.3%) contained NRSF binding sites (Figure 2A).
evidence: Analysis of the 470 repressed genes identified 39 that contain NRSE sites, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NRSE-containing genes are significantly enriched among genes repressed by KA-induced seizures compared to the total gene population.
source: The significant enrichment in the fraction of NRSE-containing genes in the repressed vs total gene population (8.3% vs 2.8%) indicated that NRSF-regulated genes were preferentially repressed by epilepsy-provoking network hyperactivity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical comparison shows 8.3% of repressed genes contain NRSE sites versus 2.8% in the total detected gene population, indicating significant enrichment.

claim: NRSF-regulated genes are preferentially repressed by epilepsy-provoking network hyperactivity.
source: The significant enrichment in the fraction of NRSE-containing genes in the repressed vs total gene population (8.3% vs 2.8%) indicated that NRSF-regulated genes were preferentially repressed by epilepsy-provoking network hyperactivity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The enrichment of NRSE-containing genes among repressed genes (8.3% vs 2.8%) provides evidence for preferential repression.

claim: Only approximately 10% of NRSE-containing genes are repressed by KA-induced seizures when NRSF levels increase twofold to threefold.
source: Whereas 371 of the detected hippocampal genes contained an NRSE and were therefore potential NRSF targets, only 39 of these were repressed by KA-induced seizures when NRSF levels increased twofold to threefold.
evidence: Microarray data shows that of 371 NRSE-containing genes, only 39 (approximately 10%) were repressed following seizures that increased NRSF levels 2-3 fold.

claim: Decoy oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) comprised of the NRSF binding sequence can bind to cellular NRSF and inhibit its ability to bind to target genes.
source: We generated oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) comprised of the NRSF binding sequence (NRSE), modified their backbone for stability and infused them into the brain. These ODNs acted as 'decoys', binding to cellular NRSF and inhibiting its ability to bind to target genes (Figure 3A) (McClelland et al., 2011a).
evidence: The decoy ODN strategy is described and supported by citation to McClelland et al., 2011a and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: NRSE-ODN administration has little effect on the expression of most genes in naive hippocampus with low baseline NRSF levels.
source: Consistent with the low baseline levels of NRSF in naive hippocampus, preventing the binding of the repressor to target genes had little effects on the expression of most of the 39 genes (compare "random ODN" and NRSE–ODN columns in the control brain, left side of Figure 3B).
evidence: Microarray data comparing control groups with random ODN versus NRSE-ODN shows minimal differences in gene expression, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Of the 39 NRSE-containing genes repressed by seizures in the presence of random ODNs, the majority (28) were no longer significantly repressed when NRSF binding to target genes was inhibited.
source: Of the 39 NRSE-containing genes that were repressed by seizures in the presence of random ODNs, (depicted in blue in Figure 3B) the majority (28) were no longer significantly repressed when NRSF binding to target genes was inhibited (compare the [KA-seizures + NRSE ODN] group to either of the control groups; Figure 3B).
evidence: Microarray data shows that 28 of 39 genes repressed by seizures were rescued (no longer significantly repressed) when NRSE-ODN was administered, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Seizure-induced repression of Myo5B is rescued by NRSE-ODN administration.
source: Several genes that were both repressed by seizure activity and rescued by interference with NRSF function were tested (Glra2, Myo5B, Stmn2), and results analyzed using two way ANOVA. Myo5B F(1,18) = 9.35, p = 0.007; Glra2 F(1,17) = 46.89, p = 0.0001; Stmn2 F(1,18) = 1.97, p = 0.047, n = 4/group.
evidence: qPCR validation with two-way ANOVA shows statistically significant rescue of Myo5B expression by NRSE-ODN (p = 0.007), as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Seizure-induced repression of Glra2 is rescued by NRSE-ODN administration.
source: Several genes that were both repressed by seizure activity and rescued by interference with NRSF function were tested (Glra2, Myo5B, Stmn2), and results analyzed using two way ANOVA. Myo5B F(1,18) = 9.35, p = 0.007; Glra2 F(1,17) = 46.89, p = 0.0001; Stmn2 F(1,18) = 1.97, p = 0.047, n = 4/group.
evidence: qPCR validation with two-way ANOVA shows statistically significant rescue of Glra2 expression by NRSE-ODN (p = 0.0001), as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Seizure-induced repression of Stmn2 is rescued by NRSE-ODN administration.
source: Several genes that were both repressed by seizure activity and rescued by interference with NRSF function were tested (Glra2, Myo5B, Stmn2), and results analyzed using two way ANOVA. Myo5B F(1,18) = 9.35, p = 0.007; Glra2 F(1,17) = 46.89, p = 0.0001; Stmn2 F(1,18) = 1.97, p = 0.047, n = 4/group.
evidence: qPCR validation with two-way ANOVA shows statistically significant rescue of Stmn2 expression by NRSE-ODN (p = 0.047), as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: qPCR analysis of NRSE-containing genes that were not repressed on the microarray shows excellent correlation with the microarray data.
source: We next examined the microarray data by performing qPCR analysis of a subset of NRSE-containing genes that were found to be repressed on the array and a second subset of genes whose expression was not altered on the array following KA-seizures (Figure 4A,B). These qPCR analyses revealed excellent correlation with the microarray and both methods distinguished between the NRSE-containing genes that were or were not repressed by seizures.
evidence: qPCR validation of genes not repressed on microarray (Atp2b, Crhr2, Ep300, Hcn2, Kcnh2, P2xr5, Pcsk1, Xpo6) confirmed the microarray findings, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: qPCR analysis of NRSE-containing genes that were repressed on the microarray shows excellent correlation with the microarray data.
source: We next examined the microarray data by performing qPCR analysis of a subset of NRSE-containing genes that were found to be repressed on the array and a second subset of genes whose expression was not altered on the array following KA-seizures (Figure 4A,B). These qPCR analyses revealed excellent correlation with the microarray and both methods distinguished between the NRSE-containing genes that were or were not repressed by seizures.
evidence: qPCR validation of genes repressed on microarray (Calb1, Glra2, Grin2a, Hcn1, Kcnc2, Klf9, Lrp11, Myo5b, Stmn2) confirmed the microarray findings, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes repressed by seizure-induced increases of NRSF levels have a large increment in NRSF binding.
source: As apparent in this figure, (a) genes repressed by seizure-induced increases of NRSF levels were those that had a large increment in NRSF binding.
evidence: ChIP analysis comparing NRSF binding before and after seizures shows that repressed genes (shown in green in Figure 5) have large increases in NRSF binding.

claim: The increment in NRSF binding at repressed genes arises on the background of moderate binding levels in the naive state.
source: In addition, (b) this increment arose on the background of moderate binding levels in the naive state.
evidence: ChIP analysis shows that genes with large increases in NRSF binding after seizures (repressed genes) had moderate baseline binding in naive hippocampus, as shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: NRSF binding to genes with modest baseline binding (Ep300, Hcn2, P2xr5, Xpo6) does not increase significantly upon seizure-induced increase of NRSF levels.
source: Specifically, the effects of seizure-induced increase of NRSF levels on NRSF binding to the chromatin correlated with the degree of repressor binding in the naive state: binding of NRSF to certain genes (Ep300, Hcn2, P2xr5, Xpo6) was modest and did not increase significantly upon seizure-induced increase of NRSF levels (white columns of Figure 5A–C).
evidence: ChIP data shows that genes with low baseline NRSF binding (white columns in Figure 5) do not show significant increases in binding after seizures.

claim: NRSF binding to genes with very robust baseline binding (Atp2b, Crhr2, Htr1a, Pcsk1) is relatively independent of NRSF tissue levels.
source: NRSF binding was very robust at NRSE sites of other genes (Atp2b, Crhr2, Htr1a, Pcsk1), and the degree of binding was relatively independent of NRSF tissue levels (black columns of Figure 5A–C).
evidence: ChIP data shows that genes with high baseline NRSF binding (black columns in Figure 5) do not show significant changes in binding after seizures despite increased NRSF levels.

claim: Seizure-induced increase of NRSF levels markedly augments NRSF binding to genes (Calb1, Glra2, Grin2A, Hcn1, Kcnc2) where binding was moderate in the naive hippocampus.
source: In contrast, seizure-induced increase of NRSF levels markedly augmented NRSF binding to genes such as Calb1, Glra2, Grin2A, Hcn1, and Kcnc2, where binding was moderate in the naive hippocampus.
evidence: ChIP data shows that genes with moderate baseline NRSF binding (green columns in Figure 5) show large increases in binding after seizures.

claim: Genes with moderate baseline NRSF binding that show increased binding after seizures are preferentially repressed by NRSF in mature hippocampus.
source: The latter set of genes was those preferentially repressed by NRSF in mature hippocampus (Figure 4B and Figure 5C).
evidence: Integration of ChIP data (Figure 5) and gene expression data (Figure 4B) shows that genes with moderate baseline binding and increased binding after seizures are those that are repressed.

claim: In genes with very low binding to NRSF, a moderate increase of NRSF levels would not alter repressor binding appreciably.
source: According to the model (Figure 6), in genes with very low binding to NRSF, a moderate increase of NRSF levels would not alter repressor binding appreciably.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data patterns, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: In genes with high binding frequency to NRSF, NRSEs would likely be occupied even by the low NRSF levels in the naive hippocampus.
source: Similarly, in genes with high binding frequency to NRSF, NRSEs would likely be occupied even by the low NRSF levels in the naive hippocampus.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data patterns, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Increased NRSF levels would be unlikely to augment occupancy or promote suppression of genes with high baseline NRSF binding.
source: Increased NRSF levels would be unlikely to augment occupancy or promote suppression of these genes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data patterns, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: When NRSF binding is mid-range, relatively small fluctuation of NRSF levels would result in major changes of repressor binding and gene repression.
source: In contrast, when NRSF binding is 'mid-range', then relatively small fluctuation of NRSF levels would result in major changes of repressor binding and gene repression.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data patterns, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: NRSF-binding scores of all hippocampal NRSE-containing genes range from 19 to 5544 with a mean of 279, median of 153, and standard deviation of 429.
source: In the overall population of NRSE-containing hippocampal genes, binding frequencies ranged from 19 to 5544 (mean 279; median 153; standard deviation 429).
evidence: Analysis of ChIP-Seq data from Johnson et al., 2007 applied to the hippocampal gene set provides these binding frequency statistics.

claim: NRSF-binding scores of genes functionally regulated by NRSF range from 27 to 663 with a mean of 214, median of 172, and standard deviation of 166.
source: In contrast, NRSF-binding scores of the genes that were functionally regulated by NRSF ranged from 27 to 663 (mean 214; median 172; standard deviation 166).
evidence: Analysis of ChIP-Seq data from Johnson et al., 2007 applied to the subset of NRSF-regulated genes identified in this study provides these binding frequency statistics.

claim: The frequency medians of all NRSE-containing hippocampal genes and NRSF-regulated NRSE-containing genes are not significantly different.
source: Whereas the frequency medians of all NRSE-containing hippocampal genes and NRSF-regulated NRSE-containing genes were not significantly different (Mann–Whitney p = 0.86), the scatter plots and regression-fit histograms demonstrated that the gene population regulated by NRSF in the context of epileptogenesis was more tightly clustered and had distinct distribution properties.
evidence: Statistical comparison using Mann-Whitney test shows no significant difference in medians (p = 0.86).

claim: The gene population regulated by NRSF in the context of epileptogenesis is more tightly clustered and has distinct distribution properties compared to all NRSE-containing genes.
source: Whereas the frequency medians of all NRSE-containing hippocampal genes and NRSF-regulated NRSE-containing genes were not significantly different (Mann–Whitney p = 0.86), the scatter plots and regression-fit histograms demonstrated that the gene population regulated by NRSF in the context of epileptogenesis was more tightly clustered and had distinct distribution properties.
evidence: Visual analysis of scatter plots and regression-fit histograms in Figure 7B,C shows tighter clustering and different distribution properties.

claim: Skewness is 6.5 in all detected NRSE-containing genes versus 1.2 in the regulated genes.
source: Skewness was 6.5 in all detected NRSE-containing genes vs 1.2 in the regulated genes; Kurtosis was 66 in all of the genes and 0.98 in the regulated genes.
evidence: Statistical analysis of binding frequency distributions provides these skewness values.

claim: Kurtosis is 66 in all detected NRSE-containing genes versus 0.98 in the regulated genes.
source: Skewness was 6.5 in all detected NRSE-containing genes vs 1.2 in the regulated genes; Kurtosis was 66 in all of the genes and 0.98 in the regulated genes.
evidence: Statistical analysis of binding frequency distributions provides these kurtosis values.

claim: NRSF-binding distribution of the total NRSE-containing hippocampal gene population is exceedingly different from normal distribution.
source: Notably, whereas NRSF-binding distribution of the total NRSE-containing hippocampal gene population was exceedingly different from normal (all: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p < 0.0001, D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test p < 0.0001), the distribution pattern of the regulated gene population was much closer to normal (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p > 0.10, D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test p = 0.012).
evidence: Statistical normality tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov and D'Agostino-Pearson) show highly significant deviation from normal distribution (p < 0.0001 for both tests).

claim: The distribution pattern of the NRSF-regulated gene population is much closer to normal distribution compared to all NRSE-containing genes.
source: Notably, whereas NRSF-binding distribution of the total NRSE-containing hippocampal gene population was exceedingly different from normal (all: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p < 0.0001, D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test p < 0.0001), the distribution pattern of the regulated gene population was much closer to normal (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p > 0.10, D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test p = 0.012).
evidence: Statistical normality tests show the regulated gene population is closer to normal distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p > 0.10, D'Agostino-Pearson p = 0.012).

claim: The population of NRSF-regulated hippocampal genes is distinct and characterized by a relatively narrow, normally-distributed range of NRSF-binding frequencies.
source: Together, these clustering patterns suggest that the population of NRSF-regulated hippocampal genes is distinct and characterized by a relatively narrow, normally-distributed range of NRSF-binding frequencies.
evidence: Statistical analyses of binding frequency distributions (skewness, kurtosis, normality tests) support this conclusion.

claim: Three gene sets with binding frequencies between the 37.5th and 75th percentile rank were significantly enriched in the control group compared to the seizure group.
source: The expression of three of these 'bins' (gene sets partitioned by binding frequency) was significantly enriched in the control group (i.e., repressed in the seizure group) when compared to the levels of enrichment of gene sets composed of random permutations of genes (FWER *p < 0.05). Notably, the three significantly enriched gene-sets were not composed of genes with the highest NRSF binding frequency; rather, they consisted of genes between the 37.5th and 75th binding frequency rank percentile (Figure 7D; Table 1; Figure 8).
evidence: GSEA analysis shows three gene sets (37.5-50%, 50-62.5%, 62.5-75% binding frequency percentiles) were significantly enriched in controls (FWER p < 0.05), as shown in Figure 7D, Table 1, and Figure 8.

claim: When NRSF function is blocked with NRSE-ODN treatment, the three binned gene sets with mid-range binding frequencies are no longer significantly different from controls.
source: In addition, when binding-frequency binned GSEA was used to compare the control group to the KA-seizure group receiving the NRSE–ODN treatment (i.e., with blocked NRSF function), the three binned gene sets were no longer significantly different from those in the control group (Table 1).
evidence: GSEA analysis comparing controls to KA-seizures + NRSE-ODN shows the three mid-range binding frequency gene sets are no longer significantly enriched, as shown in Table 1.

claim: Genes regulated by NRSF encode primarily molecules that contribute to neuronal function and plasticity.
source: Genes that were both repressed by the seizures and 'rescued' by blocking NRSF–NRSE interactions encoded primarily molecules that are well-known to contribute to neuronal function and plasticity.
evidence: Analysis of the identity of NRSF-regulated genes identified in Table 2 shows they encode ion channels, receptors, calcium-related molecules, and other neuronal function-related proteins.

claim: NRSF-regulated genes include ion channels and their accessory subunits.
source: These included ion channels and their accessory subunits, neurotransmitter receptors, genes involved in calcium-mediated cellular cascades, and phospho-enzymes (Table 2).
evidence: Table 2 lists NRSF-regulated genes including HCN1, LRP11, KCNC2, KCNIP2, BAI2, SCN3B, SLC12A5, KCNC1 which are ion channels or accessory subunits.

claim: NRSF-regulated genes include neurotransmitter receptors.
source: These included ion channels and their accessory subunits, neurotransmitter receptors, genes involved in calcium-mediated cellular cascades, and phospho-enzymes (Table 2).
evidence: Table 2 lists NRSF-regulated genes including GRIN2A, GLRA2, NTRK3 which are neurotransmitter receptors.

claim: NRSF-regulated genes include genes involved in calcium-mediated cellular cascades.
source: These included ion channels and their accessory subunits, neurotransmitter receptors, genes involved in calcium-mediated cellular cascades, and phospho-enzymes (Table 2).
evidence: Table 2 lists NRSF-regulated genes including CADPS, CALB1, HPCA, CABP7, MYO5B, CAMKV which are involved in calcium-mediated cascades.

claim: NRSF-regulated genes include phospho-enzymes.
source: These included ion channels and their accessory subunits, neurotransmitter receptors, genes involved in calcium-mediated cellular cascades, and phospho-enzymes (Table 2).
evidence: Table 2 lists NRSF-regulated genes including GNAO1, PRKCG, PRKCB1, NELL1 which are phospho-enzymes.

claim: Several NRSF-regulated genes encode transcription factors or proteins involved in signaling cascades that might influence downstream gene expression.
source: Several of these genes encode for transcription factors (e.g., Kruppel-like factor 9 [Klf9]), or proteins involved in signaling cascades that might influence downstream gene expression (Grin2A, PKC, Nell1), suggesting that they might mediate secondary (indirect) effects of NRSF.
evidence: Analysis of gene functions in Table 2 identifies KLF9 as a transcription factor and GRIN2A, PKC, NELL1 as signaling molecules.

claim: Preventing the repression of NRSF-regulated genes attenuated seizure-provoked neuroplasticity that promoted epilepsy.
source: Notably, this NRSF-regulated gene set is crucial in influencing the function of both individual neurons (Garriga-Canut et al., 2006) and neuronal network behavior. Their importance is supported by the fact that preventing their repression attenuated seizure-provoked neuroplasticity that promoted epilepsy (McClelland et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citation to McClelland et al., 2011a showing that NRSE-ODN treatment attenuated epileptogenesis.

claim: Interfering with NRSF function attenuated development of epilepsy.
source: We have previously shown that interfering with the function of the neuron-restrictive silencer factor (NRSF/REST), an important transcription factor that influences neuronal phenotype, attenuated development of this disorder.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work (McClelland et al., 2011a).

claim: Epilepsy-provoking seizures increased the low NRSF levels in mature hippocampus several fold.
source: In this study, we found that epilepsy-provoking seizures increased the low NRSF levels in mature hippocampus several fold yet surprisingly, provoked repression of only a subset (∼10%) of potential NRSF target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 showing 2-3 fold increases in NRSF mRNA and protein.

claim: Epilepsy-provoking seizures provoked repression of only a subset (approximately 10%) of potential NRSF target genes.
source: In this study, we found that epilepsy-provoking seizures increased the low NRSF levels in mature hippocampus several fold yet surprisingly, provoked repression of only a subset (∼10%) of potential NRSF target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by microarray data showing 39 of 371 NRSE-containing genes were repressed.

claim: The repressed gene-set was rescued when NRSF binding to chromatin was blocked.
source: Accordingly, the repressed gene-set was rescued when NRSF binding to chromatin was blocked.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by microarray and qPCR data showing gene rescue with NRSE-ODN treatment (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Genes selectively repressed by NRSF had mid-range binding frequencies to the repressor.
source: Unexpectedly, genes selectively repressed by NRSF had mid-range binding frequencies to the repressor, a property that rendered them sensitive to moderate fluctuations of NRSF levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP data (Figure 5) and binding frequency analysis (Figure 7).

claim: Mid-range binding frequencies render genes sensitive to moderate fluctuations of NRSF levels.
source: Unexpectedly, genes selectively repressed by NRSF had mid-range binding frequencies to the repressor, a property that rendered them sensitive to moderate fluctuations of NRSF levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the model in Figure 6 and data showing genes with mid-range binding are those regulated by moderate NRSF increases.

claim: Genes selectively regulated by NRSF during epileptogenesis code for ion channels, receptors, and other crucial contributors to neuronal function.
source: Genes selectively regulated by NRSF during epileptogenesis coded for ion channels, receptors, and other crucial contributors to neuronal function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the gene list in Table 2.

claim: Dynamic, selective regulation of NRSF target genes may play a role in influencing neuronal properties in pathological and physiological contexts.
source: Thus, dynamic, selective regulation of NRSF target genes may play a role in influencing neuronal properties in pathological and physiological contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings of the study.

claim: Epileptic networks arise via numerous mechanisms.
source: Epileptic networks arise via numerous mechanisms (Pitkänen et al., 2011; Vezzani et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012; Hildebrand et al., 2013; Rowley and Patel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Changes in neuronal properties and resulting alterations of network behavior constitute one of the important mechanisms of epileptogenesis.
source: Changes in neuronal properties and resulting alterations of network behavior constitute one of the important mechanisms of epileptogenesis (Yaari and Beck, 2002; Noam et al., 2011; Goldberg and Coulter, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Neuronal properties may change because of genetic mutations in crucial neuronal genes.
source: Neuronal properties may change because of genetic mutations in crucial neuronal genes (Meisler and O'Brien, 2012; Oliva et al., 2012; Kingwell, 2013; Papale et al., 2013) or from insult-related alterations of gene expression that affect the levels and function of their products.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Neuronal properties may change from insult-related alterations of gene expression that affect the levels and function of their products.
source: Neuronal properties may change because of genetic mutations in crucial neuronal genes (Meisler and O'Brien, 2012; Oliva et al., 2012; Kingwell, 2013; Papale et al., 2013) or from insult-related alterations of gene expression that affect the levels and function of their products.
evidence: This is supported by the context of the introduction and general knowledge.

claim: Altered expression of individual ion channels has been extensively reported in epilepsy.
source: Whereas altered expression of individual ion channels (Brewster et al., 2002; Khirug et al., 2010; Poolos, 2012; van Loo et al., 2012; Maslarova et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2013), neurotransmitter receptors (Gonzalez et al., 2013; Rojas and Dingledine, 2013), and other cellular components (Zeng et al., 2009; Maroso et al., 2011; Jimenez-Mateos et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013) have been extensively reported, the nature and mechanisms of the orchestration of these gene expression changes remain unknown
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Altered expression of neurotransmitter receptors has been extensively reported in epilepsy.
source: Whereas altered expression of individual ion channels (Brewster et al., 2002; Khirug et al., 2010; Poolos, 2012; van Loo et al., 2012; Maslarova et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2013), neurotransmitter receptors (Gonzalez et al., 2013; Rojas and Dingledine, 2013), and other cellular components (Zeng et al., 2009; Maroso et al., 2011; Jimenez-Mateos et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013) have been extensively reported, the nature and mechanisms of the orchestration of these gene expression changes remain unknown
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Altered expression of other cellular components has been extensively reported in epilepsy.
source: Whereas altered expression of individual ion channels (Brewster et al., 2002; Khirug et al., 2010; Poolos, 2012; van Loo et al., 2012; Maslarova et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2013), neurotransmitter receptors (Gonzalez et al., 2013; Rojas and Dingledine, 2013), and other cellular components (Zeng et al., 2009; Maroso et al., 2011; Jimenez-Mateos et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013) have been extensively reported, the nature and mechanisms of the orchestration of these gene expression changes remain unknown
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The nature and mechanisms of the orchestration of gene expression changes in epilepsy remain unknown.
source: Whereas altered expression of individual ion channels (Brewster et al., 2002; Khirug et al., 2010; Poolos, 2012; van Loo et al., 2012; Maslarova et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2013), neurotransmitter receptors (Gonzalez et al., 2013; Rojas and Dingledine, 2013), and other cellular components (Zeng et al., 2009; Maroso et al., 2011; Jimenez-Mateos et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013) have been extensively reported, the nature and mechanisms of the orchestration of these gene expression changes remain unknown
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: Gene expression is dynamically regulated throughout life and influences neuronal phenotype and behavior.
source: Gene expression is dynamically regulated throughout life and influences neuronal phenotype and behavior (Bale et al., 2010; Robison and Nestler, 2011; Sweatt, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Dynamic regulation of gene expression is mediated by transcriptional enhancers and repressors that bind to specific sequences of target genes and modify their expression.
source: This dynamic regulation is mediated by transcriptional enhancers and repressors that bind to specific sequences of target genes and modify their expression (Ballas et al., 2005; Kohyama et al., 2008; Hwang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: NRSF functions by binding a DNA sequence called neuron-restrictive silencer element (NRSE) to mediate long-term, cell-specific gene repression.
source: The repressor neuron-restrictive silencer factor (NRSF/ REST) functions by binding a DNA sequence called neuron-restrictive silencer element (NRSE) to mediate long-term, cell-specific gene repression (Schoenherr and Anderson, 1995) via complex interactions with co-repressors such as mSin3 and Co-Rest (Chen et al., 1998; Andres et al., 1999; Naruse et al., 1999; Roopra et al., 2001; Wood et al., 2003; Belyaev et al., 2004; Kuwabara et al., 2004; Mortazavi et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007; Abrajano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature, particularly Schoenherr and Anderson, 1995.

claim: NRSF mediates gene repression via complex interactions with co-repressors such as mSin3 and Co-Rest.
source: The repressor neuron-restrictive silencer factor (NRSF/ REST) functions by binding a DNA sequence called neuron-restrictive silencer element (NRSE) to mediate long-term, cell-specific gene repression (Schoenherr and Anderson, 1995) via complex interactions with co-repressors such as mSin3 and Co-Rest (Chen et al., 1998; Andres et al., 1999; Naruse et al., 1999; Roopra et al., 2001; Wood et al., 2003; Belyaev et al., 2004; Kuwabara et al., 2004; Mortazavi et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007; Abrajano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: NRSF is highly expressed in non-neuronal tissues where it represses neuronal genes.
source: NRSF is highly expressed in non-neuronal tissues where it represses neuronal genes (Ballas and Mandel, 2005) and has important roles in neurogenesis and neuronal differentation within the brain (Hsieh et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2008; Westbrook et al., 2008; Mandel et al., 2011; Aoki et al., 2012; Ernsberger, 2012; Kok et al., 2012; Rodenas-Ruano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ballas and Mandel, 2005.

claim: NRSF has important roles in neurogenesis and neuronal differentiation within the brain.
source: NRSF is highly expressed in non-neuronal tissues where it represses neuronal genes (Ballas and Mandel, 2005) and has important roles in neurogenesis and neuronal differentation within the brain (Hsieh et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2008; Westbrook et al., 2008; Mandel et al., 2011; Aoki et al., 2012; Ernsberger, 2012; Kok et al., 2012; Rodenas-Ruano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: NRSF levels are low in mature hippocampus.
source: NRSF levels are low in mature hippocampus where ∼600 expressed genes contain NRSEs and are thus potentially regulated by the repressor.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by baseline measurements in Figure 1.

claim: Approximately 600 expressed genes in mature hippocampus contain NRSEs and are thus potentially regulated by NRSF.
source: NRSF levels are low in mature hippocampus where ∼600 expressed genes contain NRSEs and are thus potentially regulated by the repressor.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on known NRSE-containing genes.

claim: Hippocampal NRSF expression increases several-fold following seizures.
source: Hippocampal NRSF expression increases several-fold following seizures (Palm et al., 1998; Garriga-Canut et al., 2006; McClelland et al., 2011a) and following other insults that promote epilepsy (Calderone et al., 2003; Noh et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature and data in Figure 1.

claim: NRSF expression increases following other insults that promote epilepsy.
source: Hippocampal NRSF expression increases several-fold following seizures (Palm et al., 1998; Garriga-Canut et al., 2006; McClelland et al., 2011a) and following other insults that promote epilepsy (Calderone et al., 2003; Noh et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Blocking NRSF function attenuated the epileptic phenotype induced by severe seizures.
source: We found that blocking NRSF function attenuated the epileptic phenotype induced by severe seizures (McClelland et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McClelland et al., 2011a.

claim: The contribution of NRSF to epilepsy and epileptogenesis is currently the focus of intense study.
source: The contribution of NRSF to epilepsy and its development (epileptogenesis) is currently the focus of intense study (Roopra et al., 2012; Goldberg and Coulter 2013; Pozzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Conditional deletion of NRSF in the forebrain resulted in increased susceptibility to kindling and enhanced mossy fiber sprouting.
source: Interestingly, Hu et al. found that the conditional deletion of NRSF in the forebrain resulted in increased susceptibility to kindling and enhanced mossy fiber sprouting (Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2011.

claim: Complete deletion of NRSF in naive neurons may induce large cascades of transcriptional changes rendering neurons more susceptible to seizures.
source: Complete deletion of NRSF in 'naive' neurons may induce large cascades of transcriptional changes rendering neurons more susceptible to seizures.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the findings of Hu et al., 2011.

claim: Acute disruption of NRSF function after an epilepsy-provoking insult provides a more direct approach to elucidate the epileptogenic functions of NRSF.
source: In contrast, acute disruption of NRSF function 'after' an epilepsy-provoking insult, as performed in our current and previous studies, provides a more direct approach to elucidate the epileptogenic functions of NRSF because it does not interfere with NRSF function prior to the epilepsy-inducing insult.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage of the current approach.

claim: The majority of NRSF-regulated genes are already known to contribute to crucial neuronal properties.
source: Investigating the identity of these genes, we were pleased to find that the majority were already known to contribute to crucial neuronal properties, and many had been previously implicated in pathological states including epilepsy (Sloviter, 1989; Palm et al., 1999; Pathak et al., 2007; Zuccato et al., 2007; van Gassen et al., 2009; Khirug et al., 2010; Soldati et al., 2011; McClelland et al., 2011a; Nikitidou et al., 2012; Kingwell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genes in Table 2 and citations to the literature.

claim: Many NRSF-regulated genes had been previously implicated in pathological states including epilepsy.
source: Investigating the identity of these genes, we were pleased to find that the majority were already known to contribute to crucial neuronal properties, and many had been previously implicated in pathological states including epilepsy (Sloviter, 1989; Palm et al., 1999; Pathak et al., 2007; Zuccato et al., 2007; van Gassen et al., 2009; Khirug et al., 2010; Soldati et al., 2011; McClelland et al., 2011a; Nikitidou et al., 2012; Kingwell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The binding of NRSF to a gene is required for its repression.
source: The binding of NRSF to a gene is required (though not always sufficient; [Belyaev et al., 2004]) for its repression.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle with citation to Belyaev et al., 2004.

claim: The binding of NRSF to a gene is not always sufficient for its repression.
source: The binding of NRSF to a gene is required (though not always sufficient; [Belyaev et al., 2004]) for its repression.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Belyaev et al., 2004.

claim: The specific NRSE sequence can influence the degree of NRSF binding.
source: A number of mechanisms may influence both the degree of NRSF binding as well as the degree of its repressive effect on genes. These include the specific NRSE sequence (Mortazavi et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2007) that is unlikely to be the cause in the current studies (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mortazavi et al., 2006 and Johnson et al., 2007.

claim: The interaction of NRSF with co-factors can influence the degree of NRSF binding and repressive effect.
source: Other important mechanisms include the interaction of NRSF with co-factors (Andres et al., 1999; Naruse et al., 1999; Wood et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2011), as well as additional, still enigmatic effects of the chromatin environment of individual genes (Belyaev et al., 2004), which might be influenced by 'super-enhancers' (Lovén et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The chromatin environment of individual genes can influence the degree of NRSF binding and repressive effect.
source: Other important mechanisms include the interaction of NRSF with co-factors (Andres et al., 1999; Naruse et al., 1999; Wood et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2011), as well as additional, still enigmatic effects of the chromatin environment of individual genes (Belyaev et al., 2004), which might be influenced by 'super-enhancers' (Lovén et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Super-enhancers might influence the chromatin environment effects on NRSF binding.
source: Other important mechanisms include the interaction of NRSF with co-factors (Andres et al., 1999; Naruse et al., 1999; Wood et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2011), as well as additional, still enigmatic effects of the chromatin environment of individual genes (Belyaev et al., 2004), which might be influenced by 'super-enhancers' (Lovén et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is proposed with citations to Lovén et al., 2013 and Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: There is a correlation between repressor occupancy and gene repression.
source: Here, we examined the binding of NRSF to hippocampal genes before and after an epilepsy-provoking insult and found significant increment in genes that were repressed by the factor. This suggested a correlation between repressor occupancy and gene repression (Hammar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 5 and citation to Hammar et al., 2014.

claim: Genes with the strongest binding probability for NRSF would likely be constitutively bound to and suppressed by NRSF.
source: Traditionally, the focus of studies on gene–repressor interaction has been on genes with the strongest binding probability (Nichols et al., 1992; Chen et al., 1998; Singh et al., 2002). However, the genes with the strongest binding for NRSF would likely be constitutively bound to—and suppressed by—NRSF.
evidence: This is proposed based on the data and supported by citations to traditional approaches.

claim: Genes with the strongest NRSF binding are unlikely to respond to moderate changes in NRSF levels.
source: These genes are unlikely to respond to moderate changes in NRSF levels.
evidence: This is proposed based on the model and data showing high-binding genes do not change expression with moderate NRSF increases.

claim: Relatively modest seizure-induced changes in NRSF levels regulate a subset of NRSE-containing genes that fall within a moderate dynamic range of NRSF binding probabilities.
source: Rather, relatively modest seizure-induced changes in the tissue levels of NRSF regulate a subset of NRSE-containing genes that fall within a moderate 'dynamic range' of NRSF binding probabilities.
evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the integration of binding frequency data (Figure 7) and gene expression data.

claim: Changes in NRSF levels are moderate in ischemia.
source: This concept may be important for other forms of insult-induced plasticity in the mature brain including ischemia (Noh et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2014), peripheral nerve injury (Uchida et al., 2010), and seizure-induced epilepsy (McClelland et al., 2011a; Goldberg and Coulter, 2013) where changes in NRSF levels are moderate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Noh et al., 2012 and Kaneko et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in NRSF levels are moderate in peripheral nerve injury.
source: This concept may be important for other forms of insult-induced plasticity in the mature brain including ischemia (Noh et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2014), peripheral nerve injury (Uchida et al., 2010), and seizure-induced epilepsy (McClelland et al., 2011a; Goldberg and Coulter, 2013) where changes in NRSF levels are moderate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uchida et al., 2010.

claim: Changes in NRSF levels are moderate in seizure-induced epilepsy.
source: This concept may be important for other forms of insult-induced plasticity in the mature brain including ischemia (Noh et al., 2012; Kaneko et al., 2014), peripheral nerve injury (Uchida et al., 2010), and seizure-induced epilepsy (McClelland et al., 2011a; Goldberg and Coulter, 2013) where changes in NRSF levels are moderate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McClelland et al., 2011a and Goldberg and Coulter, 2013, and data in Figure 1.

claim: The role of NRSF in mature brain is distinct from its role in development.
source: These findings support a role of NRSF in mature brain that is distinct from its role in development, when NRSF contributes to neuronal identity by repressing neuronal genes in non-neuronal tissues (Schoenherr and Anderson, 1995; Coulson, 2005), and specifies neuronal fate (Kuwabara et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings and supported by citations to the literature on NRSF's developmental roles.

claim: During neuronal differentiation, NRSF levels plunge, de-repressing genes that contribute to neuronal identity.
source: In that context, large changes in the expression of NRSF take place: NRSF levels plunge during neuronal differentiation (Gates et al., 2010; Ernsberger, 2012), de-repressing genes that contribute to neuronal identity (Wood et al., 2003; Belyaev et al., 2004; Abrajano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The gene set regulated by moderate changes in NRSF expression consists of molecules important for neuronal function and plasticity during development.
source: Remarkably, the gene set regulated by moderate changes in NRSF expression in the current study consisted of molecules which are extremely important for neuronal function and plasticity not only during development (Gates et al., 2010; Juliandi et al., 2010; Rodenas-Ruano et al., 2012; Pernhorst et al., 2013), but also in the adult brain (Lepagnol-Bestel et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2011; Pernhorst et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The gene set regulated by moderate changes in NRSF expression consists of molecules important for neuronal function and plasticity in the adult brain.
source: Remarkably, the gene set regulated by moderate changes in NRSF expression in the current study consisted of molecules which are extremely important for neuronal function and plasticity not only during development (Gates et al., 2010; Juliandi et al., 2010; Rodenas-Ruano et al., 2012; Pernhorst et al., 2013), but also in the adult brain (Lepagnol-Bestel et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2011; Pernhorst et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Insult-induced increases of NRSF levels and activity contribute to epileptogenesis via NRSF-mediated repression of a group of genes that critically influence neuronal function.
source: In summary, insult-induced increases of NRSF levels and activity contribute to epileptogenesis via NRSF-mediated repression of a group of genes that critically influence neuronal function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the findings of the study.

claim: The basis of the selective regulation of a subset of NRSE-containing genes includes their mid-range binding frequencies to NRSF.
source: The basis of the selective regulation of a subset of NRSE-containing genes includes their mid-range binding frequencies to NRSF, so that moderate fluctuations in NRSF levels influence the degree of their binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ChIP and binding frequency analyses.

claim: Moderate fluctuations in NRSF levels influence the degree of binding to genes with mid-range binding frequencies.
source: The basis of the selective regulation of a subset of NRSE-containing genes includes their mid-range binding frequencies to NRSF, so that moderate fluctuations in NRSF levels influence the degree of their binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ChIP data showing increased binding at mid-range genes after moderate NRSF increases.

claim: These findings inform about the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in the mature hippocampus.
source: These findings inform us about the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in the mature hippocampus.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the broader implications of the findings.
